newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli cabinet in key session on budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: Israeli cabinet in key session on budget cuts.

text.p: The Israeli government convened on Monday to decide on further budget cuts which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said were needed to put the economy back on track and maintain Israel's financial position abroad.

"If we don't cut, let there be no doubt that we will pay with a deterioration in our standing in the financial markets and in our credit rating," a statement quoted Netanyahu as telling the cabinet session.

Netanyahu said Finance Minister Dan Meridor was seeking additional cuts of 1.2 billion shekels ($366 million), on top of the 4.9 billion shekels of cutbacks included in the original 1997 budget of 190.8 billion shekels.
On the eve of the session, Treasury sources had put the extra cuts at some 1.8 billion shekels.
"We are presenting another cut because it became clear to us that revenues have not met our expectations," Meridor told Israel Radio.
"Today, the world is watching us -- investors, banks and governments -- to see...whether the government will fix what has gone wrong in the economy in the last two years," he said.
Economists said government revenues have fallen below projections and the prospect of increased government borrowing has pushed up interest rates, strengthened the shekel and sucked in imports.
As a result Israel's current account deficit is expected to widen to more than $5 billion this year from $4.1 billion in 1995.

"I think the finance minister has done exceptional work and he has found several sources (of income), which do not involve raising taxes, worth over half a billion shekels," Netanyahu said, without giving details.
"But that still leaves us with a significant cut and he will present this 1.2 billion shekel cut," Netanyahu said.

Treasury sources said the proposals included the already announced sale of government-owned homes in Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank, a move certain to draw Arab and international ire. Some 3,000 homes will be sold.
Netanyahu accused the Labour government which he defeated in May elections of managing the economy "terribly" and said his administration would "correct the financial system".
Former prime minister Shimon Peres dismissed the criticism, telling Israel Radio: "They were four wonderful years for the Israeli economy, it grew like yeast".
Legislators have said the reductions, widely reported to target spending on social welfare and education, would hit lower-income Israelis hardest.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, a self-proclaimed champion of the underprivileged and a key coalition partner, has declined to say if he would support the cuts.
Other than pledging not to raise taxes for now, the Treasury had not publicly given precise details of the new budget package, pending the cabinet debate.
"The cut will be very deep. I don't think there has been a cut like this one in the last 10 years," Netanyahu's economic adviser Moshe Leon said as the cabinet met.
The final budget package will go to parliament for debate and a ratification vote before December 31.
($1=3.28 shekels)
